findings.title: OAuth single-flight is broken: the losing Task is created (and starts) before the CAS, so concurrent callers each run their own refresh-token exchange
findings.evidence: OpenAIProvider.refreshAndWriteBack L106-128 (same code in AnthropicProvider.swift L96-116): `if let existing = refreshFlight.withLock({ $0 }) {...}` then `let task = Task<CodexAuth, Error> { defer { refreshFlight.withLock { $0 = nil } }; let resp = try await OpenAIOAuth.refresh(refreshToken: auth.tokens.refreshToken, http: http) ... try credentials.writeBack(updated) }`, and only after that `refreshFlight.withLock { slot in if let existing = slot { return existing }; slot = task; return task }`. An unstructured Task starts running as soon as it is created. Losing the CAS only throws away the handle; it does not stop the exchange. The loser's `defer` also sets the slot to nil while the winner is still running.
findings.impact: With manage_oauth_refresh=true (opt-in), two overlapping fetches both POST the same refresh_token. Both vendors rotate the RT on every exchange, so the second exchange reuses a consumed RT. That gives invalid_grant, and with reuse detection the whole token family is revoked (forced re-login in both the app and the CLI). If both exchanges succeed, the two writeBacks race and can leave an RT the server has already replaced. The loser's defer also re-opens the slot, so a third exchange can start.
findings.fix: Create and store the Task inside one withLock critical section: return the existing Task, or create the new one and store it in the same closure. In the defer, clear the slot only if it still holds this task (compare handles). Apply to both providers.
findings.failure_scenario: A scheduled tick starts fetch A (token within refreshBuffer). 50 ms later the user clicks refresh. VendorViewModel cancels A's Task, but that cancel does not reach the code between read() and refreshAndWriteBack, and the refresh Task is unstructured anyway. A and B both read slot==nil at L106 and both create Tasks at L109, so two OpenAIOAuth.refresh POSTs go out with the same RT. A installs its task. B finds A's task and awaits its value, but B's orphan Task keeps running, exchanges the already-consumed RT, and its defer sets slot=nil.

test_red_green.name: refreshFlight_concurrentCallers_exchangeOnce
test_red_green.assert_before: StubURLProtocol counts POSTs to the token endpoint and holds each response on a barrier. Start two fetchUsage(forceRefresh:true) calls concurrently with an expiring id_token and manageOAuthRefresh=true, then release the barrier. Expect tokenEndpointHits == 1. FAILS today (2).
test_red_green.assert_after: tokenEndpointHits == 1; the auth.json RT equals the single response's refresh_token; both callers return the same access token.

findings.cetico_evidence: The check and the store are not atomic. OpenAIProvider.swift:106 reads the slot, :109 creates Task{} (it runs at once, because the provider is a final class and not an actor, so nothing serializes it), and only :123-127 stores it. AnthropicProvider.swift:92-113 has the same shape. Downgraded from HIGH: (1) only reachable with opt-in manage_oauth_refresh=true; (2) fetchUsage has a single caller, VendorViewModel.swift:226, which cancels the previous task before starting the next (:222). (3) The window between the two withLock calls is only as long as Task creation (microseconds). The finding's own scenario (a click 50 ms later) does NOT produce a double exchange: by then B finds A's Task in the slot and joins it.

findings.title: A refresh can use a refresh_token another caller already rotated (credential read before the await, no re-read or CAS inside the flight)
findings.evidence: OpenAIProvider fetch closure: `var auth = try credentials.read()` (L68) ... `return try await fetchUsageBytes(auth: auth)` ... `catch AppError.http(401, _) where manageOAuthRefresh && !didRefresh { ...; auth = try await refreshAndWriteBack(auth) }` (L92-94). refreshAndWriteBack exchanges the `auth.tokens.refreshToken` that was captured before the network await. Once an earlier flight has finished and cleared the slot (defer L110), a late caller starts a new exchange with the pre-rotation RT. AnthropicProvider.loadCredentials L82-90 has the same shape: credentials are read before `refreshAndWriteBack(credentials)`.
findings.impact: Opt-in mode: the second exchange sends an RT that was already rotated. The server returns invalid_grant and may revoke the token family, so both the Codex CLI and the app are logged out.
findings.fix: Inside the single-flight task, re-read the credential. If its refresh_token differs from the one the caller passed in, someone already rotated it: return the fresh credential and skip the exchange. Alternatively, key the flight by the RT being rotated and memoize the result for that RT.
findings.failure_scenario: Fetches A and B run with the same access token (A from the scheduled tick, B from the auth.json watcher or scheduleReauthRetry). A gets a 401 at t=300 ms, refreshes, writes back, and clears the slot at t=700 ms. B's 401 arrives at t=750 ms because of network jitter. The slot is nil, so B calls refreshAndWriteBack(authOld) and runs a second exchange with RT_old, which is already consumed.

test_red_green.name: reactive401_lateCaller_doesNotReuseRotatedRT
test_red_green.assert_before: Stub the usage endpoint to return 401 to two requests, releasing the second only after the first refresh has finished. Stub the token endpoint to return invalid_grant for any RT it has already seen. Expect B to succeed. FAILS today: B throws invalid_grant and the token endpoint is hit twice.
test_red_green.assert_after: The token endpoint is hit exactly once; B retries the usage call with the rotated access token and succeeds.

findings.cetico_evidence: There is no re-read of the credential inside the flight: OpenAIProvider.swift:68 reads auth before the await, and :94 exchanges the captured RT. A vector is possible: A gets a 401, passes checkCancellation (:93) and starts the flight. B supersedes A and reads auth.json before A's writeBack (:120). B's usage call gets a 401 after A's flight has cleared the slot, so B exchanges RT_old. That needs the server to revoke the AT, a user or watcher refresh landing inside the exchange window, and the opt-in flag. Anthropic is mostly immune: its 401 path calls invalidateCachedCredentials and re-reads (AnthropicProvider.swift:66-68). Not proven.

findings.title: The scheduler skips the whole tick whenever any vendor is .loading, so one fetch that never completes stops scheduled refresh for ALL vendors
findings.evidence: RefreshScheduler L116-118: `if self.store?.isAnyVendorLoading == true { continue }`. This skips markScheduledTick and refreshAll for every vendor and sleeps another full interval. Nothing limits how long a vendor can stay .loading. AntigravityExecutor.swift L80-103 wraps the child process in `withCheckedThrowingContinuation`, which does not respond to cancellation, and blocks on `stdout.fileHandleForReading.readDataToEndOfFile()`. The 35 s timer only sends `process.terminate()` (L88): there is no SIGKILL and no pipe close. A child that ignores SIGTERM, or a grandchild that inherited stdout, leaves the continuation unresumed indefinitely. Cancelling the Task from VendorViewModel.refresh does not resume it either.
findings.impact: One hung vendor freezes usage for every vendor (menu-bar %, notifications, history) with no error shown. The countdown stays at 0:00 because lastScheduledTickAt is never re-stamped. Even without a hang, one slow vendor at tick time makes every other vendor wait an extra full interval (300 s).
findings.fix: Make the gate per-vendor: skip only vendors whose own refresh is in flight (VendorViewModel already cancels on supersede), or limit the skip by a maximum in-flight age. In AntigravityExecutor, escalate from terminate to SIGKILL after a grace period, close the read ends on timeout, drain stdout and stderr concurrently, and use withTaskCancellationHandler to terminate the child and resume the continuation on cancel.
findings.failure_scenario: At the t=0 tick, agy spawns a helper that inherits stdout and stays alive. readDataToEndOfFile never returns and the vendor's state stays .loading. At t=300, 600, ... isAnyVendorLoading is true, so the loop hits continue. Anthropic, OpenAI and the rest never refresh again until relaunch.

test_red_green.name: scheduler_hungVendor_doesNotStarveOthers
test_red_green.assert_before: UsageStore with two stub providers: A's fetchUsage awaits a continuation that is never resumed, B counts its calls. RefreshScheduler(minimumInterval: 0.05). After 0.3 s expect B.calls >= 3. FAILS today (1).
test_red_green.assert_after: B keeps being refreshed every interval; A is skipped or timed out on its own.

findings.cetico_evidence: The gate is real: RefreshScheduler.swift:116-118 skips every vendor if any one is .loading. But no unbounded fetch is shown. HTTP is capped by timeoutIntervalForResource=30 s (HTTPClient.swift:17). The security tool has a 5 s budget plus SIGKILL (SecurityToolCredentialReader.swift:163-168). agy is capped at 35 s by SIGTERM (AntigravityExecutor.swift:83-89). All of these finish well under the 300 s interval. I ran the real ~/.local/bin/agy the same way the app does: 1781 B stdout, 0 B stderr, exited normally, and the --bg-updater child it spawned exited within a few seconds (it never inherited the pipe). A permanent hang needs agy to ignore SIGTERM or a descendant to hold the pipe; neither was observed.

findings.title: Anthropic planLabel() reads the Keychain (or runs /usr/bin/security) synchronously on the cooperative pool while holding credentialMutationGate
findings.evidence: AnthropicProvider.planLabel L152-157: `if let cached { return cached.label }; guard let credentials = try? credentialReader.read() else { return nil }`. It is called from decodeSnapshot. CachedFetch.run calls decodeSnapshot synchronously inside an async function, on both the cache-hit path (CachedFetch.swift L26-27) and the stale-fallback path (L105-106). KeychainCredentialReader.read() holds the NSRecursiveLock credentialMutationGate across SecItemCopyMatching. On an ACL fast-fail it also runs SecurityToolCredentialReader.runTool while holding the lock, which can wait up to 5 s + 1 s + 1 s + 1 s. CLAUDE.md requires that blocking read to hop off the pool via readOffPool().
findings.impact: At launch (labelCache empty, fresh disk cache), the first decode can block a cooperative-pool thread for up to ~8 s on ad-hoc builds, where the fallback is the normal read path. Every other reader (the fetch path's readOffPool, authorize) waits behind the gate. A failed read leaves labelCache nil, so every cache hit tries again.
findings.fix: Never read credentials from decode. Pass in the label computed in the fetch closure (primeLabelCache already runs there), or make planLabel return only the memoized value. Alternatively, call readOffPool before decode from an async context.
findings.failure_scenario: Launch within the cache TTL: fetchUsage -> freshPayloadWithAge hit -> decodeSnapshot -> planLabel -> read() -> direct read fails with -25308 -> security tool subprocess runs for 5 s on a cooperative thread. Meanwhile the status store and the other providers' tasks queue on the reduced pool.

test_red_green.name: planLabel_cacheHit_doesNotCallBlockingRead
test_red_green.assert_before: Reader stub whose read() sleeps 2 s and records the calling thread and call count. Seed a fresh DiskCache and call fetchUsage(forceRefresh:false). Expect read() call count == 0 on the cache-hit path. FAILS today (1 call, on a pool thread).
test_red_green.assert_after: decode never calls read(); the label is nil or memoized; the fetch returns in < 50 ms.

findings.cetico_evidence: CachedFetch.swift:26-27 on a cache hit calls decodeSnapshot, which calls planLabel (AnthropicProvider.swift:157), which calls a synchronous credentialReader.read(). That read holds credentialMutationGate (KeychainCredentialReader.swift:53-54) and can hit the security-tool fallback (:186-192) on a cooperative thread. This breaks the readOffPool rule in CLAUDE.md. Downgraded: it happens once at launch, when labelCache is empty. After a fallback failure the 1 h / 5 min cooldown makes later attempts return fast, so the cost is at most about 5-8 s on one pool thread.

findings.title: Codex auth.json writeBack can lose a concurrent Codex CLI update: the file contents read before the OAuth network await are written back unchanged
findings.evidence: OpenAIProvider L68 `var auth = try credentials.read()` -> await OpenAIOAuth.refresh (a network call of hundreds of ms) -> FileCredentialReader.writeBack L57-73 `var blob = updated.unknownTopLevel ... blob["tokens"] = ...; try AtomicFileWrite.write(data, to: path, permissions: 0o600)`. Before the replace there is no re-read, no mtime or content check, and no advisory lock shared with the CLI.
findings.impact: Opt-in mode: if the Codex CLI rewrites auth.json during our exchange (its own refresh, or `codex login` to another account), we overwrite its newer tokens and account with ours plus our stale unknownTopLevel. The CLI's freshly rotated RT is lost, so either the CLI is logged out or the file points at a different account than the CLI expects.
findings.fix: Re-read auth.json before replacing it. If its tokens differ from the ones the exchange started from, someone else rotated: keep the disk version and discard ours. Otherwise merge only the tokens object into the freshly read file. In effect, a compare-and-swap on the pre-exchange refresh_token.
findings.failure_scenario: t0: the app reads auth.json (RT1). t0+50 ms: the `codex` CLI refreshes RT1->RT2 and writes auth.json. t0+400 ms: the app's exchange with RT1 (perhaps accepted in a grace window) returns RT3, and writeBack replaces the file with RT3 plus stale top-level keys. The CLI holds RT2 in memory while disk now has RT3.

test_red_green.name: writeBack_doesNotClobberConcurrentCLIWrite
test_red_green.assert_before: Stub the token endpoint to hold on a barrier. While it is held, overwrite auth.json with a different refresh_token and an extra top-level key, then release. Expect the disk refresh_token to equal the CLI's value and the extra key to survive. FAILS today.
test_red_green.assert_after: Disk keeps the CLI's newer tokens and keys; the provider returns the disk credentials.

findings.cetico_evidence: The scenario needs the Codex CLI to be rewriting auth.json at the same time as the app's opt-in refresh. CLAUDE.md Hard rules say manage_oauth_refresh=true is 'opt-in, standalone use without that CLI', and the default is read-only (OpenAIProvider.swift:39 manageOAuthRefresh=false). Concurrent writes with the CLI fall outside the supported configuration, so this is a documented decision, not a defect.

findings.title: FileCredentialReader.read() can clear the pending copy based on a stale verdict (check-then-act across two lock sections)
findings.evidence: L37 `let pending = state.withLock { $0.pendingUpdate }` ... L50-51 `if verdict.dropPending { state.withLock { $0.pendingUpdate = nil } }`. The lock is released between reading pending and clearing it, so writeBack's failure path (`state.withLock { $0.pendingUpdate = updated }` in the catch) can run in between.
findings.impact: Opt-in mode: a just-rotated credential whose write failed is the only surviving copy of the new RT. It gets dropped, and the next read serves the pre-rotation RT from disk, which logs the user out.
findings.fix: Clear only if the value is unchanged: `state.withLock { if $0.pendingUpdate == pending { $0.pendingUpdate = nil } }` (compare tokens). Or do the whole reconcile inside one lock section.
findings.failure_scenario: Thread A in read(): disk D (exp=T1), pending=nil, so the verdict picks disk. Thread B's writeBack fails and sets pending=P (exp=T2>T1). A sees dropPending == true and sets pending=nil. P is lost.

test_red_green.name: fileReader_readRacingFailedWriteBack_keepsPending
test_red_green.assert_before: Inject a disk-read hook that pauses read() between L37 and L50 on a barrier. Meanwhile run writeBack to an unwritable path, then resume. Expect the next read() to return P. FAILS today (returns D).

findings.cetico_evidence: The stated scenario (pending=nil at read time, then dropPending==true) is impossible. With disk present and pending nil, pick returns dropPending:false (FileCredentialReader.swift:154-155). dropPending is true only when a pending copy existed AND disk is at least as fresh (:150-151). In the supported standalone mode that only happens after our own successful writeBack, and that already clears pending (:76). The leftover interleave needs a second concurrent failed writeBack, which the single-caller model rules out.

findings.title: CreditBaselineStore.reset() does not take writeGate, so a record() already in flight re-saves the old peak and silently undoes Recalibrate
findings.evidence: record() L192-213 holds `writeGate` from `let stored = load()` through `save(updated)`, but `public func reset() { cached.withLock { $0 = nil }; try? FileManager.default.removeItem(at: fileURL) }` takes no writeGate. decodeSnapshot (OpenAIProvider L163-183) calls store.record on every decode, including cache hits and stale fallbacks.
findings.impact: A decode running at the same time can revert the user's 'Recalibrate credits bar': the old high-water mark comes back and the bar keeps showing the wrong consumed %. Separately, if the forced refresh that follows recalibration fails, the stale fallback decodes the cached payload and re-seeds the baseline from a balance that may be days old.
findings.fix: Take writeGate in reset(). Optionally skip record() for stale-fallback decodes.
findings.failure_scenario: Fetch thread in record(): load() returns stored (peak 10000). Main thread: recalibrateCredits -> reset() clears the cache and the file. Fetch thread: save(peak 10000). On the next refresh the peak is 10000 again.

test_red_green.name: creditBaseline_resetDuringRecord_isNotReverted
test_red_green.assert_before: Two actors: A calls record() with a load hook paused on a barrier; B calls reset(); then release. Expect load() == nil afterwards. FAILS today (the old peak is restored).
test_red_green.assert_after: After reset completes, the baseline is nil or seeded only from observations that started after the reset.

findings.cetico_evidence: reset() does skip writeGate (CreditBaseline.swift:244-247 vs :193). But record() writes only if stored != updated (:206). A concurrent 'keep' decode with unchanged flags therefore never re-saves the old peak. A revert needs the concurrent decode to also change has_credits/promo or push the balance past the peak, in the same microseconds as the click. recalibrateCredits then forces a refresh (VendorSectionView.swift:569-570), which re-seeds anyway.

findings.title: AntigravityExecutor reads stdout to EOF before reading stderr, so more than 64 KB on stderr blocks the child until the 35 s timer
findings.evidence: L101-103: `let outData = stdout.fileHandleForReading.readDataToEndOfFile(); let errData = stderr.fileHandleForReading.readDataToEndOfFile(); process.waitUntilExit()`. The pipes are drained one after the other: the child blocks writing to a full stderr pipe while we block waiting for stdout EOF.
findings.impact: Verbose agy stderr output (stack traces, debug logs) turns a successful call into a 35 s hang and a misleading timeout error, and a GCD worker is tied up the whole time.
findings.fix: Drain stderr concurrently, using a readabilityHandler or a second DispatchQueue read, as SecurityToolCredentialReader already does for stdout.
findings.failure_scenario: agy writes 100 KB to stderr, then JSON to stdout, then exits. Its stderr write blocks at 64 KB while our thread waits for stdout EOF. The timer terminates the child at 35 s and the call fails with timedOut.

test_red_green.name: antigravity_largeStderr_noDeadlock
test_red_green.assert_before: Point the executor at a script that prints 200 KB to stderr and '{}' to stdout. Expect completion in < 2 s. FAILS today (~35 s, timeout error).

findings.cetico_evidence: AntigravityExecutor.swift:101-103 drains stdout to EOF, then stderr, then waits. If stderr goes over the pipe buffer, the call blocks until the 35 s SIGTERM (:88) and then fails with a timeout. The damage is bounded: the call ends at 35 s. Measured with the real agy: 0 B stderr, so there is no trigger today.

findings.title: SecurityToolCredentialReader sends SIGKILL by bare PID after the child may already have been reaped (PID-reuse race)
findings.evidence: L164-168: `process.terminate(); if exited.wait(timeout: .now() + 1) == .timedOut { kill(process.processIdentifier, SIGKILL) ...}`. `exited` is signalled from terminationHandler, which Foundation runs after it reaps the child. The child can already be reaped, freeing its PID, while the handler is still queued, so a timed-out wait does not prove the PID is still ours.
findings.impact: Theoretical: SIGKILL could hit an unrelated process of the same user that reused the PID within about 1 s.
findings.fix: Check `if process.isRunning { kill(...) }` right before the kill, which shrinks the window to negligible. Or kill only while the child is known to be unreaped, e.g. via kqueue EVFILT_PROC.
findings.failure_scenario: security exits at t=5.9 s after SIGTERM and Foundation reaps it. terminationHandler is queued behind a busy queue, so wait(1 s) times out at t=6.0. A new process has reused the PID, and kill(SIGKILL) hits it.

test_red_green.name: securityTool_timeout_doesNotKillAfterReap
test_red_green.assert_before: Hard to reproduce deterministically. Through a Process seam, assert that kill is skipped when isRunning == false after terminate.
test_red_green.assert_after: No kill is sent once the child is no longer running.

findings.cetico_evidence: The premise of PID reuse within about 1 s does not hold on macOS. PIDs are handed out in sequence and wrap at 99999, so reusing one inside the 1 s window (SecurityToolCredentialReader.swift:165-167) would take roughly 100k forks in that second. The window between Foundation reaping the child and running terminationHandler is milliseconds.

findings.title: AtomicFileWrite creates the tmp file with umask permissions and chmods it afterwards (brief 0644 window), which contradicts its own doc comment and the 'at write time' rule
findings.evidence: L19-25: `try data.write(to: tmp, options: .atomic)` then `try FileManager.default.setAttributes([.posixPermissions: ...], ofItemAtPath: tmp.path)`. The tmp file (and the inner temp file Foundation creates for .atomic) is created with the default 0644 mode and already holds the full payload before the chmod.
findings.impact: If the directory is traversable, another local user can open the tmp file between creation and chmod. This applies to the auth.json write-back in ~/.codex (opt-in) and to history and cache files. The 0700 Application Support directory already protects most callers.
findings.fix: Create the tmp file with open(O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_WRONLY, 0o600), or FileManager.createFile(atPath:contents:attributes:[.posixPermissions: 0o600]), write through that fd, then rename.
findings.failure_scenario: The writer calls data.write, so the tmp file exists at 0644 with the token in it. A reader running as another account opens it. The writer then chmods it to 0600, but the reader's open fd keeps access.

test_red_green.name: atomicWrite_tmpNeverWorldReadable
test_red_green.assert_before: Run a watcher that stats every new '.auth.json.*.tmp' in the directory during 1000 writes. Expect no mode other than 0600. FAILS today.
test_red_green.assert_after: Every tmp file observed has mode 0600 from creation.

findings.cetico_evidence: AtomicFileWrite.swift:19-24 calls data.write(.atomic), which creates the file under the umask (0644), and only then setAttributes 0600. ~/.codex is 0755 and ~ is 0750 with group staff, so another staff user can reach the tmp file during that window. Only the opt-in auth.json writeBack is exposed. Everything under Application Support is protected by its 0700 directory (verified with ls -ld).

findings.title: The initial history load in VendorViewModel init can overwrite a sample recorded by a refresh that finished first
findings.evidence: L151-156: `Task { @MainActor [weak self] in let samples = await Task.detached(priority: .utility) { store.load(since: cutoff) }.value; self?.history = samples }`, versus recordHistory L274-284: `store.append(...); var current = history; current.append(sample); history = ...`. Nothing orders the two.
findings.impact: On a fast cache-hit launch, the newest sparkline point disappears until the next refresh (transient UI only).
findings.fix: Merge instead of assigning: `self.history = (samples + self.history)`, deduplicated and sorted. Or record that the load has completed and have recordHistory append only after it.
findings.failure_scenario: The detached load reads the JSONL at t=5 ms. A cache-hit refresh completes at t=8 ms, appends to the file and sets history=[..., s_new]. The load returns at t=20 ms with samples that lack s_new, and history=samples drops it.

test_red_green.name: vendorVM_initialLoad_doesNotDropRecordedSample
test_red_green.assert_before: Stub a history store whose load() blocks on a barrier. Trigger a refresh so recordHistory runs, then release the load. Expect history.last == s_new. FAILS today.
test_red_green.assert_after: history contains both the loaded samples and s_new.

findings.cetico_evidence: VendorViewModel.swift:151-155 assigns history = samples after the detached load, while recordHistory (:275-284) appends on its own. On a fast cache-hit launch, the load can read the file before the append, so the new sample is lost. The effect is transient and UI-only.
